Geopolitics.title: Canadian PM Mark Carney discusses talks with the EU, overdependence on the US and how to deal with Donald Trump in a DW interview.
Geopolitics.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney tells DW that Canada is seeking closer EU ties to "diversify and deepen" partnerships beyond the Americas. Despite German pushback, he said he favors the all-new term "associate membership."

Geopolitics.title: Bollywood and the underworld — together in the spotlight?
Geopolitics.summary: A wave of shootings and extortion threats has rattled India's film industry. This time, those claiming responsibility are very different from the Mumbai underworld that had Bollywood in its grip back in the 1990s.

Geopolitics.title: PSG secure 9th consecutive win thanks to Achraf Hakimi hat-trick
Geopolitics.summary: A night to remember for PSG in Le Havre. In the opening fixture of Ligue 1's ninth round, the French champions thrashed Le Havre at the Stade Océane, inspired by an outstanding performance from Achraf Hakimi. The Moroccan star scored a hat-trick and provided two assists, playing a decisive role in all five of his team's goals. PSG strengthened their grip on top spot, while Le Havre remain rooted to the bottom of the table.

Science.title: Chemists develop AI tool to convert human ingenuity into life-enhancing enzymes
Science.summary: Many have voiced concerns that artificial intelligence will take jobs away from humans. But assistant professor of chemistry Zhongyue (John) Yang, along with his former doctoral student Qianzhen Shao (now a postdoc at Stanford) and other team members, has created an AI tool that aims to elevate the work that scientists do—not replace them.

Science.title: Young Canadians focus on mental health at key climate trial
Science.summary: At a landmark Canadian trial focused on the government's obligations to fight climate change, the young plaintiffs suing Ottawa over alleged policy failures have sought to focus attention on their mental health.

Science.title: Ultracold atoms simulate hard-to-observe matter-antimatter pair production
Science.summary: According to quantum electrodynamics, the theory describing interactions between light and electrically charged particles, a sufficiently strong electric field can, in principle, convert some of its energy into particles and their antimatter partners. A particle's antimatter partner has the same mass and, for electrically charged particles, the opposite electric charge.

Science.title: Hidden erosion: Study reveals soft mountain rock erodes three times faster than hard rock—with climate implications
Science.summary: A University of Massachusetts Amherst-led research team has discovered that weaker rock in mountain landscapes erodes three times faster than harder rock—even on gentler slopes—and is one of the main attributes governing mountain erosion. The finding also challenges our current understanding of the relationship between erosion and the release of carbon dioxide, and suggests that geologists and atmospheric scientists may be underestimating the CO₂ contributions coming from the Earth's rocky places.

Science.title: Why do people prefer human empathy despite rating AI empathy higher?
Science.summary: More people are turning to artificial intelligence (AI)-powered chatbots for companionship and to address loneliness. But can AI-generated empathy replace human connection?

Science.title: Scientists smash oxygen nuclei to recreate matter from the Big Bang
Science.summary: Scientists have recreated a primordial state of matter from the dawn of the universe by colliding oxygen nuclei at nearly the speed of light. The surprising results show that this exotic substance can form in smaller, lower-energy collisions than previously demonstrated, challenging the known boundaries of early-universe physics.

Science.title: New gel fuel could make rocket and satellite propulsion easier to control
Science.summary: A kerosene-based gel developed by Concordia researchers could make rocket and satellite fuels easier to store and control.

Science.title: Ghostly statue of 'shrine maiden' discovered at 1,500-year-old burial mound in Japan
Science.summary: Archaeologists have unearthed a human-shaped funeral offering that may represent an ancient Japanese priestess.

Science.title: Why it could be a bad idea to get AI to flirt for you
Science.summary: You finally started an online conversation with a stranger you find attractive, yet you don't really know what to say. They seem happy to talk, but you struggle to find the correct responses. You worry that their patience is growing thin. You pray for some guidance. Luckily, the solution could be just a few clicks away.

Science.title: For many, striped bass fishing is a way of life. But the iconic species could face collapse
Science.summary: Striped bass fishing has been Bill Jakob's passion for more than 60 years, and he remembers an era when he'd spend all night casting his line into the crashing waves off Montauk and get eight or nine fish ranging up to 40 pounds (18 kilograms), a big catch by anyone's standards.

Science.title: This oddball reflective lava world is challenging to understand
Science.summary: Among Kepler and TESS's many surprising exoplanet discoveries are the ultra-short-period (USP) planets. These planets move very quickly and complete an orbit in less than 24 hours. Ancient astronomers thought that Mercury was so fast—it goes around the sun every 88 days—that they named it after the Roman god Mercury, who was the fast-traveling messenger of the gods. They couldn't have known how sluggish Mercury is compared to the USPs.

Science.title: Scientists discover a bacterial defense so strange they thought it was broken
Science.summary: Scientists have discovered a bizarre bacterial defense system that works almost completely backward from anything seen before. Unlike typical bacterial immune systems that keep a deadly toxin under control until a virus attacks, this unusual mechanism waits until an infection begins before producing the DNA that switches on its lethal weapon. The infected bacterium then destroys itself, preventing the virus from multiplying and spreading to neighboring cells.

Science.title: Rare fossil discovery reveals new dinosaur species that specialized in eating fruit
Science.summary: Among the ravenous carnivores and lumbering herbivores that roamed the Cretaceous landscape, another kind of dinosaur was evolving that started to eat something else: the plants that began to flower and produce fruit. The discovery by paleontologists from Stony Brook University, Royal Ontario Museum (ROM) and the North Dakota Geological Survey reveals that a new species, Infernogallus jamesi—a type of small oviraptorosaur—had chewing muscles for mashing soft food, making it the first known dinosaur that specifically ate fruit.

Science.title: Scientists discover metals that defy the deep freeze at -424°F
Science.summary: Scientists have discovered a surprising mechanism that allows certain metals to resist cracking at temperatures as low as -253°C (-424°F), when similar materials typically become dangerously brittle. Instead of breaking, two experimental alloys reorganize their internal structures, creating new ways to absorb stress and remain flexible.

Science.title: A surprising vitamin A discovery is changing what scientists know about vision
Science.summary: Scientists at Johns Hopkins University have uncovered a surprising process that helps humans develop sharp vision before birth, challenging decades of assumptions about how the eye forms. Using miniature human retinas grown in the lab, researchers discovered that a vitamin A derivative and thyroid hormones work together to shape the foveola, the tiny region at the center of the retina responsible for our sharpest vision.

Science.title: White Dwarfs Aren’t Just White. Scientists Discover Dying Stars Turning Pink and Green
Science.summary: Astronomers find that a white dwarf’s density and the kind of material it absorbed from its surroundings can produce a rainbow of shades in the star’s atmosphere.

Science.title: Looking for bats after dark can help science—and change how we see them
Science.summary: What's that chirping sound coming through the detector? Did you feel something whiz past? Those are just some ways people react when they encounter microbats for the first time. Microbats are small, mostly nocturnal mammals that use ultrasonic sounds to navigate and hunt at night. They do this through echolocation, producing calls and listening to the echoes that bounce back from objects and prey.

Science.title: Rare Iron Age Celtic helmet discovered in northeastern Poland far from its homeland
Science.summary: Around 2,400 years ago, at Łysa Góra in Poland, a group of people took a bronze helmet, crushed it, broke it into pieces and threw it into a pit with iron adzes and a scythe. Such helmets are sometimes found in lavish graves of the Celtic warrior elite, from Champagne, France, to Dürrnberg, Austria.

Science.title: Four new frog species reveal more of Peru's biodiversity
Science.summary: Science can't study a species—or unlock its potential to change the world—until people actually know it exists. Four new species of frogs have now been given names, thanks to the efforts of FIU biologist Alessandro Catenazzi.

Science.title: Giant virus yields potassium channel gene that illuminates complex protein evolution
Science.summary: Researchers have discovered a gene for a tandem potassium channel in an algal virus. The finding supports the view that giant viruses may have contributed significantly to the evolution of complex proteins. The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Science.title: A simple blood test could reveal Alzheimer’s risk 10 years before symptoms
Science.summary: A major international study found that a simple blood test could help predict Alzheimer’s-related cognitive decline years before symptoms appear, with the highest-risk individuals facing a 38% chance of impairment within five years and an estimated 78% chance within 10 years. Scientists believe the discovery could pave the way for earlier intervention and future treatments designed to prevent Alzheimer’s before memory problems begin.

Science.title: Spatial mapping reveals how human urogenital organs codevelop during organogenesis
Science.summary: A new study has mapped human urogenital development in its native spatial context, revealing how neighboring organs coordinate their development through cellular communication and molecular signaling during embryogenesis.

Science.title: 75,000-year-old Neanderthal may have been killed by a spear aimed at the heart
Science.summary: A Neanderthal who died 75,000 years ago may have been killed by a wooden spear deliberately aimed at the heart, revealing rare evidence of prehistoric violence. A circular hole in the shoulder blade suggests the weapon pierced the chest and caused a rapidly fatal injury. Surprisingly, the same individual had survived an earlier devastating facial injury, suggesting other Neanderthals provided care and support.

Science.title: What the Cornell 7 sexual assault allegations reveal about how parents talk to their kids about rape
Science.summary: There is approximately 60 years of research on campus sexual assault and shelves full of books on young people's sexual experiences and behaviors, including their experiences with assault.

Science.title: Astronomers may have been wrong about what ended the 'Cosmic Dark Age'
Science.summary: How did the universe transition from an impenetrable fog of hydrogen into the bright and starlit cosmos we see today? Astronomers think they're onto the answer.

Science.title: A mysterious 4,000-year-old wall is rewriting North Africa’s history
Science.summary: A remarkable 4,000-year-old defensive structure discovered in Morocco is rewriting what scientists thought they knew about ancient North African civilizations. The massive fortifications reveal unexpectedly sophisticated prehistoric societies and suggest that the region played a much greater role in Mediterranean history than previously recognized.

Science.title: New home for orangutans rescued from Indonesia's burning forests
Science.summary: Deep in a forest in Indonesian Borneo, conservationists open a cage. A female orangutan and her baby waste little time, clambering up the towering trees and disappearing into the canopy, safe at last.

Science.title: Tiny photonic chip links telescopes together to view the universe in 'astonishing' detail
Science.summary: A tiny glass chip developed by researchers at Heriot-Watt University has linked two telescopes together to enable them to act as a single powerful instrument, marking an important step toward a new generation of astronomical technology.

Science.title: Figuring out where cosmic neutrinos come from is tricky—radio telescopes could help find 'ghost particles' origin
Science.summary: Neutrinos are funny little particles that weigh almost nothing, making them one of the universe's most elusive building blocks. They can come from objects as mundane as bananas and as exotic as supernovas—the exploding death throes of massive stars. Most neutrinos stream through space and pass through the Earth without interacting with anything.

Science.title: Calling species 'invasive'—and culling them—isn't done lightly. But it matters to Australia's threatened species
Science.summary: It may sound abstract, but distinctions between "native," "introduced" or "invasive" species can often be life or death. Species considered invasive in Australia—such as European rabbits and feral pigs—are often culled, while most native animals are generally left alone.

Science.title: Nations commit to get nature goals back on track
Science.summary: Nearly 200 nations struck hard-fought agreements Friday at a U.N. biodiversity summit, but the outcome was accompanied by disappointment over missed opportunities to address humanity's destructive toll on nature.

Science.title: Can animals lie? This sneaky bird might be proof.
Science.summary: In his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats," biologist James O'Hanlon surveys deception across the animal kingdom and asks whether any of it adds up to lying.

Science.title: Livestock guardian dogs enlisted in efforts to conserve Texas' smallest fox
Science.summary: In the Texas Panhandle, two livestock guardian dogs patrol a herd of cattle grazing the Rita Blanca National Grasslands. Although their singular focus is protecting the herd from would-be predators, their presence may make them wildlife conservation allies.

Science.title: Four superconducting cables link two large quantum processors into one
Science.summary: As quantum computers grow more ambitious, many researchers believe the best way forward is to build them in multiple interconnected parts. In these modular designs, separate quantum processors are linked so they can work together as one larger machine. For this to happen, however, connections must carry fragile quantum information without destroying it.

Science.title: 'You start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches': A biologist on whether animals can lie
Science.summary: Writer Olivia Maule spoke with biologist James O'Hanlon about his book "Liars, Cheats and Copycats."

Science.title: Are narcissists multiplying or is the social media algorithm making them bolder? The answer in five stages
Science.summary: Social media doesn't necessarily reflect who you are, but it may intensify particular personality traits and confirm or even persuade you that your worst behavior is justified.

Science.title: Novel chemical reaction expands options for building DNA-encoded libraries
Science.summary: Finding new drugs requires screening vast numbers of compounds to identify those that interact with a biological target. DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) help researchers explore these large collections by attaching a short DNA sequence to each molecule, acting as a molecular barcode that allows compounds with promising properties to be identified.

Science.title: Chemists create disappearing tattoos: Here's the science behind how they work
Science.summary: How handy would it be if you could make your tattoos invisible for a job interview in the morning, and reveal them again for a party in the evening? This sounds like science fiction, but it may soon be reality.

Science.title: Hauntology examines how what happened in the past—and what didn't—informs the present
Science.summary: The spooky is a hugely popular phenomenon in British culture, demonstrated in what now seems like a month-long Halloween celebration, a rich tradition of horror cinema and a growing interest in the uncanny. But there are other manifestations of haunting.

Science.title: 'Molecular armor' can trap shape-matched planar molecules
Science.summary: A research team has designed and synthesized a molecular cage with an internal cavity by connecting two curved π-conjugated molecules face-to-face at three points.

Science.title: Scientists develop new system to boost prime editing in dicot plants
Science.summary: A new gene-editing system could make it easier for researchers to introduce precise genetic changes into crops such as tomatoes, soybeans and rapeseed. Developed by researchers in China, SmartPE improves prime editing efficiency in several dicot plants, addressing a major limitation of the technique.

Science.title: How a 'tropical' shortcut could help particle collider experiments
Science.summary: Particle accelerators are expensive. Not just to build or to run, but also to predict the outcome of measurements obtained from them.

Science.title: Are sharks really older than trees?
Science.summary: It seems like a simple question, but it needs serious taxonomic sleuthing. Are sharks or trees the oldest?
